content.intro: This lesson develops topic 20 of the supplied curriculum: **Array Strides and Memory Layout**. The main starting point is **What strides represent**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Shape describes how values are arranged; dtype describes how values are represented. Inspecting both before an operation catches many mistakes early.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Array Strides and Memory Layout** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **What strides represent** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)
print(a.flags.c_contiguous)

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Strides describe the byte steps used to move along axes. They depend on element size and layout; inspect `strides` and `flags` before assuming an array is contiguous.

common_mistakes.why: Size counts elements; shape describes axis lengths.
Slicing and transposing can produce non-contiguous views.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect `flags` and `strides` when memory layout matters.
